Know Your Financial Position

Before you can manage money well, you need an honest picture of where you stand. In this module you build two simple personal financial statements, a net worth sheet and a monthly cash flow statement, and then score your financial health with five numbers you can recheck every quarter.
Your personal balance sheet: assets, debts and net worth
List everything you own that has money value and everything you owe
Calculate your net worth with one subtraction
Tell the difference between an asset that earns, one that holds value and one that loses value
Explain why net worth matters more than income alone

Most money advice starts with income: how much comes in each month. Income matters, but it only tells you about the flow of money. It does not tell you what you have built. Two women can each earn about ₦150,000 a month. One owns a sewing machine, a plot of land and some savings, and owes nothing. The other owes a loan app and a cooperative, and owns very little. Their income is the same, but their **financial position** is very different. The tool that shows this position is called a **personal balance sheet**, or a net worth statement.
A woman reviewing her personal finances on a large screen
A balance sheet is a snapshot of everything you own and owe on one day.
Three words you need

**Asset**: anything you own that has money value. Cash, money in a bank or wallet app, savings in a cooperative, land, a shop's stock, equipment such as a freezer or sewing machine, livestock, gold jewellery.
**Liability**: any money you owe. A bank loan, a loan app balance, money borrowed from a relative, unpaid stock taken on credit from a supplier, rent you owe the landlord.
**Net worth**: what is left when you subtract everything you owe from everything you own. **Net worth = total assets minus total liabilities.**

Net worth can be positive or negative. A negative number does not mean you are a bad person. It simply means that today your debts are bigger than what you own. The value of the balance sheet is that it turns a vague worry into a clear number you can work on.
Valuing what you own honestly

The rule is simple: write the amount you could **realistically get if you sold it this month**, not what you paid. A freezer bought for ₦250,000 three years ago may only sell for about ₦120,000 today. Clothes, phones and furniture lose value quickly, so many planners leave everyday household items out completely and only list things that could genuinely be sold. For land, use what similar plots in the same area are selling for, and be cautious. For a cooperative, use your savings balance, not your expected payout.

Worked example: Ngozi's net worth on 1 March
For example, Ngozi sells foodstuff in a market in Enugu. She sits down with a notebook to list what she owns and owes. All naira amounts are illustrative.
Assets: cash at home ₦18,000; bank account ₦62,000; Opay wallet ₦9,500; cooperative savings ₦140,000; stock in her shop (at cost) ₦230,000; deep freezer (resale value) ₦110,000.
Liabilities: cooperative loan balance ₦180,000; money borrowed from her sister ₦50,000; supplier credit for rice ₦75,000.

Ngozi's net worth is ₦264,500. She also notices that more than half of her assets (₦370,000) are stock and cooperative savings that she cannot turn into cash quickly, which tells her she needs more easy-to-reach savings.
Why the trend matters more than the number

One balance sheet is a photograph. Several balance sheets, done on the same date every three months, become a film. If Ngozi's net worth goes from ₦264,500 in March to ₦310,000 in June, she knows her money habits are building wealth, even if some weeks felt tight. If it falls, she can look at which line moved: did a loan grow, or did stock run down without being replaced?

Repaying debt also raises net worth, even though your cash goes down. Paying ₦50,000 back to her sister lowers Ngozi's cash by ₦50,000 and lowers her liabilities by ₦50,000, so net worth stays the same on the day. But next month she no longer needs to repay that money, and that frees future income.
Keep it private and keep it updated

Write your balance sheet in a notebook you keep safe or in a locked note on your phone. Do not post it in groups or share account balances with people you do not fully trust. Pick a fixed date, such as the first day of January, April, July and October, to update it.
Business and household together?
If your business and household money are mixed, list them together for now, but mark business items with a B. In later lessons you will see why separating them gives you clearer numbers.

Your monthly cash flow statement and savings rate
Build a one-page cash flow statement from a month of real records
Group spending into fixed, variable and occasional costs

Your balance sheet shows where you stand. Your **cash flow statement** shows how you got there. It is a summary of all the money that came in and went out over one period, usually a calendar month. Companies prepare one every year in their accounts. You can prepare a simple version on one page from the records you keep in a notebook, a spreadsheet or the transaction history of your bank and wallet apps.
A person reading financial charts and figures
A cash flow statement turns a month of small transactions into a few clear totals.
Where to find a month of real numbers

**Bank and wallet statements**: most Nigerian bank apps and wallets such as Opay, Moniepoint and PalmPay let you download or view a statement for a date range. Every transfer, airtime purchase and POS payment is already recorded.
**Your notebook**: cash spending is not in any app, so it must be written down the same day.
**Receipts and invoices**: school fees, rent receipts, electricity tokens and supplier invoices.
**Memory, last**: estimates from memory are usually too low, so use them only to fill gaps and mark them as estimates.
Transfers between your own accounts are not income or spending. If you move ₦20,000 from your bank to your wallet, leave it out, or you will count the same money twice.

Occasional costs are the line most people forget. If school fees for two children are about ₦180,000 per term and there are three terms a year, the yearly cost is ₦540,000. Divided by 12, that is ₦45,000 a month. Showing that ₦45,000 every month stops fees from feeling like a shock.
Savings rate: the most useful single number

Your **savings rate** is the share of your income that you keep. **Savings rate = (money saved or used to reduce debt) divided by money in, times 100.** A rate of 10% means you keep ₦10 of every ₦100. There is no single correct rate for everyone. What matters is that it is positive and that you can see whether it rises or falls.

If your statement shows a **deficit**, the gap was covered somehow: by borrowing, by spending savings or by taking money out of business stock. Write down which one it was. A deficit covered by a loan app is far more urgent than one covered by a small dip into savings, because the loan carries interest and must be repaid from next month's income.
Worked example: Aisha's February cash flow
For example, Aisha is a nurse in Kano who also sells perfume oils on WhatsApp. She builds her February statement from her bank app, her Moniepoint wallet and her notebook. Amounts are illustrative.
Money in: salary ₦185,000 + perfume profit ₦42,000 = ₦227,000.
Fixed costs: rent share ₦40,000 + data ₦6,000 + cooperative loan repayment ₦25,000 = ₦71,000.
Variable costs: food ₦68,000 + transport ₦22,000 + electricity ₦12,000 + other ₦15,000 = ₦117,000.
Occasional costs as a monthly share: school fees ₦20,000 + gas ₦4,000 = ₦24,000.
Savings rate: she saved the ₦15,000 surplus and also repaid ₦25,000 of loan principal, so (15,000 + 25,000) ÷ 227,000 × 100 = about 17.6%.
Aisha has a surplus of ₦15,000 and an effective savings rate of about 17.6%. She sees that food is her largest variable cost and decides to test buying grains in bulk once a month.
Irregular income: use a three-month view

If your income changes a lot, one month can mislead you. Put three months side by side. Use the **lowest** month's income as your planning figure for fixed costs, and treat anything above it as money to save or to put toward occasional costs. For example, if a hairdresser earned ₦140,000, ₦95,000 and ₦160,000 in three months, she plans her fixed costs around ₦95,000, not around the average of about ₦131,667.

Protect your statements

Bank statements show your account number, balances and who pays you. Never send them to strangers or to anyone who contacts you claiming to help with a loan. Download them yourself inside your own app.

A doctor does not judge your health from one test. She checks blood pressure, weight, temperature and more, then looks for the reading that needs attention first. Money works the same way. With the balance sheet from lesson one and the cash flow statement from lesson two, you already have everything you need to calculate five simple indicators.
A woman ticking items on a large checklist
Five numbers, checked every quarter, tell you which part of your finances needs attention first.

Indicator
How to calculate it
What it tells you
1. Savings rate
Money saved or used to cut debt ÷ money in × 100
Whether you are building or standing still

**Essential monthly costs** means only what you must pay to live and work: food, rent, transport, utilities, school costs and loan repayments. It leaves out treats and celebrations. **Easy-to-reach savings** means money you can get within a few days without a penalty: cash, bank or wallet savings, not land or shop stock.

The **debt to assets** ratio needs one more word of explanation. If you own ₦500,000 of assets and owe ₦200,000, then 40% of what you own was really paid for with borrowed money. The lower this share, the more of your assets truly belong to you, and the more room you have if you ever need to borrow for a good reason.
Reading the results

Many financial educators suggest aiming, over time, for emergency savings covering three to six months of essential costs, and for a debt repayment ratio low enough that one bad month does not force new borrowing. Treat these as direction, not as rules. A woman starting from zero emergency cover is doing well if she reaches two weeks, then one month.
If emergency cover is below one month, every shock becomes a new loan. Building a small buffer usually comes first.
If the debt repayment ratio is high, a large part of every month's income is gone before it arrives. Module 2 shows you how to reduce debt in an organised order.
If debt to assets is above 100%, you owe more than you own, so net worth is negative. Stop new borrowing except in a true emergency.
If the savings rate is negative, you are spending more than you earn, often by borrowing or running down stock. Go back to your cash flow statement and find the biggest variable cost.
Worked example: Halima's quarterly check
For example, Halima is a teacher in Abuja with a small poultry side business. Her numbers for the quarter are illustrative.
Savings rate: she kept ₦12,000 and repaid ₦30,000 of loans from income of ₦210,000: 42,000 ÷ 210,000 × 100 = 20%.
Emergency cover: easy-to-reach savings ₦45,000; essential monthly costs ₦150,000: 45,000 ÷ 150,000 = 0.3 months, about nine days.
Debt repayment ratio: repayments ₦30,000 ÷ income ₦210,000 × 100 = about 14%.
Debt to assets: liabilities ₦160,000 ÷ assets ₦520,000 × 100 = about 31%.
Net worth trend: ₦360,000 now minus ₦335,000 last quarter = up ₦25,000.

Four indicators are moving in the right direction. Her weak point is emergency cover, about nine days. Her first priority is to raise easy-to-reach savings to one month of essential costs, ₦150,000, before taking any new loan for the poultry business.
Quarterly money health check
Savings rate positive?
Emergency cover above one month?
Repayments under control?
Owe less than you own?
Net worth rising?
Answer each question yes or no; the first no is usually your first priority.
Choosing your one priority

It is tempting to fix everything at once, but plans with five goals usually fail. Take the first indicator that gets a no in the checklist and make it your focus for the next three months. Write one sentence: "By 30 June I will raise my emergency cover from nine days to one month by saving ₦35,000 a month in a separate account." One clear sentence is easier to keep than a long list of intentions.

Repeat the check every quarter on the same date you update your balance sheet. Over a year you will have four readings of each indicator, and you will be able to see real progress, or catch a problem early.
A note on honesty
These numbers are only for you. If you round them to look better, you lose the main benefit, which is seeing clearly. Use real figures, mark estimates, and correct them next time.

Interest, Credit and Protection: The Tools of Money

This module gives you the arithmetic and the products behind good financial decisions. You learn how interest and inflation really work, how to read and reduce debt, how credit history follows you in Nigeria, and how insurance, pensions and regulated savings products protect what you build.
The arithmetic of money: interest, compounding and inflation
Calculate simple and compound interest on savings or a loan
Convert a monthly or daily rate into a yearly picture
Use the rule of 72 to estimate doubling time
Work out whether savings are beating rising prices

Every savings account, loan, investment and price increase is driven by the same few calculations. Banks and lenders do these calculations every day. When you can do them too, even roughly on your phone calculator, you can no longer be confused by attractive-sounding rates. This lesson covers four tools: simple interest, compound interest, rate conversion and real return.
A person using a large calculator
Your phone calculator is enough for every calculation in this lesson.
Simple interest

**Simple interest** is paid only on the original amount, called the **principal**. The formula is: **interest = principal × rate × time**. If you save ₦100,000 at 10% a year simple interest for 3 years, the interest is 100,000 × 0.10 × 3 = ₦30,000, and you end with ₦130,000.
Compound interest

**Compound interest** is interest on the principal **plus** the interest already earned. Each year the interest is added, and next year's interest is calculated on the bigger amount. Using the same ₦100,000 at 10% a year compounded yearly: after year 1 you have ₦110,000; after year 2, 110,000 × 1.10 = ₦121,000; after year 3, 121,000 × 1.10 = ₦133,100. Compounding earned an extra ₦3,100 compared with simple interest. Over 10 or 20 years the gap becomes very large. Compounding works against you in exactly the same way when unpaid loan interest is added to what you owe.
Monthly and daily rates hide the real cost

Many loans in Nigeria, especially from loan apps and some informal lenders, quote a rate per month or even per day. A small-looking number can be very expensive over a year. A rate of 4% a month is 48% a year even before compounding. If unpaid interest compounds monthly, it becomes about 60% a year, because 1.04 multiplied by itself 12 times is about 1.60. A rate of 1% a day for a 30-day loan is about 30% for that single month.

Rough yearly cost (simple)
With monthly compounding

Always ask a lender: what is the total amount I will repay, in naira, and over how many weeks or months? Comparing total repayment is easier and safer than comparing rates.

The same conversion works in your favour on savings. When a product says interest is added monthly or daily, the yearly growth is slightly higher than the quoted yearly rate, because each small payment of interest starts earning too. When comparing two savings products, ask for the effective yearly rate, sometimes written as the annual percentage yield, so you compare like with like.
The rule of 72

To estimate how long money takes to double at a yearly compound rate, divide 72 by the rate. At 12% a year, 72 ÷ 12 = about 6 years. At 8%, about 9 years. The same rule shows how fast a debt doubles if you do not pay: a debt growing at 24% a year doubles in about 3 years.
Inflation and real return

**Inflation** is the general rise in prices over time. Nigeria's official inflation rate is published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) every month. When prices rise faster than your savings grow, your money buys less, even though the naira figure went up. The return after accounting for inflation is called the **real return**.
Worked example: is Blessing's savings account keeping up?

For example, Blessing keeps ₦200,000 in a savings account paying 5% a year. Suppose prices rise by 20% over the same year. These rates are illustrative, so use the current figures from your bank and the NBS.
Savings after one year: 200,000 × 1.05 = ₦210,000.
Goods that cost ₦200,000 at the start of the year now cost 200,000 × 1.20 = ₦240,000.
Buying power: 210,000 ÷ 240,000 = 0.875, so her money buys 87.5% of what it bought a year earlier.
Real return: 0.875 minus 1 = minus 12.5%.

Blessing's balance grew by ₦10,000, but in real terms she lost about 12.5% of her buying power. Short-term emergency money still belongs somewhere safe and easy to reach, but money for goals several years away needs a product that aims to grow faster than prices, which Lesson 3 introduces.
Checking any rate in four steps
Note rate and period
Convert to a yearly rate
Find total naira cost
Compare with inflation
Run any savings offer or loan through these four steps before you agree to it.
Returns that are too good to be true

If someone promises 20% or 30% a month with no risk, the arithmetic of the rule of 72 says the money would double every few months. No legitimate business can do that for long. Promises like this are a classic sign of a Ponzi scheme. Check whether the operator is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) before giving money.

Credit is not good or bad on its own. A loan that buys stock you can sell at a profit within weeks can build your business. A loan that pays for a party, then forces you to borrow again to repay it, can trap a household for years. This lesson gives you three skills: reading the true cost of a loan, protecting your credit history, and getting out of debt in an organised way.
A person making a card payment
Every repayment you make, or miss, can follow you into your credit history.
Flat rate or reducing balance?

Lenders calculate interest in two common ways. With a **flat rate**, interest is charged on the full original amount for the whole loan, even though you are paying it down. With a **reducing balance**, interest is charged only on what you still owe, so it gets smaller each month. Two loans with the same quoted rate can cost very different amounts.
Worked example: two offers for ₦200,000 over 6 months
For example, Funmi needs ₦200,000 for stock. Lender A charges 5% per month flat. Lender B charges 5% per month on a reducing balance with equal monthly payments. These are illustrative offers.
Lender A interest: 200,000 × 0.05 × 6 = ₦60,000. Total repaid ₦260,000, or about ₦43,333 a month.
Lender B monthly payment (from a standard loan calculator): about ₦39,403. Total repaid about ₦236,421.
Lender B first month: interest 200,000 × 0.05 = ₦10,000, so about ₦29,403 reduces the debt. By month six, interest is only about ₦1,876.
Difference: 260,000 minus 236,421 = about ₦23,579 more with the flat rate.
Both lenders said 5% a month, but the flat-rate loan costs about ₦23,579 more. Funmi asks every lender for the total repayment in naira and a repayment schedule before she signs.
Your credit history in Nigeria

When you borrow from a bank, microfinance bank or many licensed lenders, your loan and how you repay it can be reported to credit bureaus licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). The licensed private bureaus include CRC Credit Bureau, FirstCentral Credit Bureau and CreditRegistry. Your records are linked to identifiers such as your BVN. A future lender can check this history, and late or unpaid loans can lead to refusal or higher rates.
You can request your own credit report from a bureau. Check each bureau's website for how to apply and any fee.
Check that every loan listed is really yours and that repaid loans show as closed. Ask the bureau and the lender to correct mistakes in writing.
Paying on time, every time, is the main way to build a good record.
Making a debt payoff plan

If you have several debts, list them all in one table with the amount owed, the interest rate and the minimum payment. Always pay the minimum on every debt. Then put any extra money on one debt at a time, using one of two well-known methods.

With the avalanche method, extra money goes to the loan app first, because it costs ₦4,800 a month. With the snowball method, extra money goes to the sister first, because clearing a whole debt quickly can give motivation. If a debt carries a very high rate, like the loan app here, the avalanche order usually saves the most. Whichever you choose, once a debt is cleared, add its payment to the next one.

If you can see that you will miss a payment, contact the lender **before** the due date. Explain what happened, propose an amount you can truly pay and ask for any new arrangement in writing. Many banks, microfinance banks and cooperatives prefer a restructured plan to a default. Do not take a new loan to repay an old one unless it is clearly cheaper and you have a plan to stop borrowing.
Digital loans: check before you borrow

The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) regulates digital and online lenders and publishes a list of approved lenders on its website. Before installing a loan app, check that it is on the list. Do not give an app access to your contacts or photos, never pay an upfront fee to receive a loan, and report harassment or threats to the FCCPC.
A simple borrowing test

Before any loan, write down: what the money is for, how it will produce the repayment, the total naira cost and what you will do if repayment is late. If you cannot answer the second question, the loan is likely to add pressure, not reduce it.

Budgeting and saving build money. Protection stops one event from wiping it out. A hospital stay, a fire in a shop or a husband's sudden death can take years of savings in a week. In Nigeria many people rely on family and community support in such moments, and that support is valuable, but it is not always enough or available. Three formal tools help: insurance, pensions and regulated long-term savings.
A closed umbrella
Insurance is like an umbrella: you pay for it in good weather so it is ready for the storm.
Insurance: sharing risk

Insurance works by pooling. Many people each pay a small, regular amount called a **premium**. When one of them suffers a covered loss, the insurer pays a claim from the pool. Insurance companies in Nigeria are licensed and supervised by the **National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)**. Some useful types for women and small businesses are:

**Health insurance**: the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) oversees health insurance nationally, and many states run their own health insurance agencies with plans for informal workers. Ask your state agency or a nearby primary health centre what plans are available.
**Micro-insurance**: low-premium cover sold through banks, cooperatives or mobile platforms, for example cover for shop stock, hospital cash or funeral costs.
**Life insurance**: pays your named beneficiaries if you die during the cover period, so children's school costs can continue.
Before you buy, read what is **excluded**, how to make a claim, how long payment takes and whether the insurer appears on NAICOM's list of licensed operators.

Once you have a policy, keep the policy document, premium receipts and the insurer's claims contact together with your other important papers. Tell your beneficiaries that the policy exists and where the papers are. If something happens, report it to the insurer as soon as possible, take photos of any damage and keep copies of everything you send. A claim is much easier when the paperwork is ready.
Pensions: income for later life

Nigeria's Contributory Pension Scheme is regulated by the **National Pension Commission (PenCom)**. Each person has a **Retirement Savings Account (RSA)** managed by a licensed Pension Fund Administrator (PFA). For employees covered by the Pension Reform Act 2014, the minimum contribution is 10% of monthly pay from the employer and 8% from the employee. If you are employed, check your RSA statement through your PFA's app or website to confirm contributions are arriving.

Most women in trading, farming and services are self-employed, so no employer contributes. PenCom's **Micro Pension Plan** lets self-employed and informal sector workers open an RSA and contribute amounts that suit them, as often as they choose. Under the plan, part of the contributions can be accessed for emergencies, according to the rules your PFA explains. Name your beneficiaries when you open the account and update them if your family changes.

For example, Comfort is a 38-year-old tailor in Port Harcourt who opens a Micro Pension account. She pays ₦60,000 at the start of each year (₦5,000 a month). Assume an illustrative return of 10% a year; real returns vary and are not guaranteed.

Financial Independence, Good Partnerships and Your Plan

The final module turns knowledge into protection and action. You secure your own financial identity and records, learn to deal confidently with banks, cooperatives and other providers, and assemble everything into a Personal Financial Management Plan with a clear 90-day path.
Financial independence: your own accounts, records and next of kin
Set up the basic financial identity every adult woman needs
Create a household asset and document register
Recognise signs of financial control in a relationship and plan safe responses
Name next of kin and beneficiaries on your accounts

Many women contribute to household money, through salaries, trading, farming or unpaid work that saves the family money, but have little control over it or little record of it. When a marriage ends, a husband dies or a family dispute starts, a woman without her own account, her own records and her name on property can lose what she helped build. Financial independence does not mean keeping secrets from your partner. It means you can act, prove and protect your share if you ever need to.
A woman organising personal documents in folders
Your own documents and records are the foundation of financial independence.
Your financial identity
**National Identification Number (NIN)** from NIMC, needed for bank accounts, SIM registration and many government services.
**Bank Verification Number (BVN)**, linked to every bank account you open. One BVN covers all your banks.
**At least one account in your own name only**, at a licensed bank or microfinance bank, with your own phone number linked to it and your own PIN that you never share.
**Your own email address and phone number** for alerts, so messages about your money come to you.

If your business is registered with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), keep a copy of the certificate and open the business account in the business name. Keeping business money separate from household money makes your records clearer and makes it easier to show what the business has earned.
The household asset and document register

A register is a simple list of every important asset and where the proof is kept. It should include land and property documents, vehicle papers, bank and pension accounts, insurance policies, cooperative passbooks and any money owed to you. Write who paid for each item, or what share you contributed. Keep originals in a safe place and copies, or phone photos, in a second safe place, such as a secured cloud folder or with a trusted relative.
Worked example: Amaka's register

For example, Amaka and her husband in Onitsha bought a plot and built a shop together. She has receipts in different bags and drawers. She spends one Saturday building a register. Amounts are illustrative.

She lists five items: the plot (receipt and survey plan in her husband's name, she contributed ₦800,000 of ₦2,000,000), the shop building (she paid ₦350,000 for roofing, receipts kept), her savings account, her Micro Pension RSA and her cooperative passbook.
She calculates her share of the plot: 800,000 ÷ 2,000,000 × 100 = 40%.
She photographs each receipt and document and saves them in a password-protected folder on her phone.
She speaks with her husband calmly about adding her name to the plot documents, and they agree to visit a lawyer together.
She writes the date of the register and a reminder to update it every six months.
Amaka now has proof of a 40% contribution to the plot, the roofing receipts for the shop and a list of every account. If a dispute ever arises, she is not relying on memory.

When money is used to control

Sometimes a partner or relative controls money in a harmful way: taking all of a woman's earnings, refusing her access to any money, forcing her to take loans in her name, or stopping her from working. This is often called **financial abuse**. It is not a normal family disagreement. If this is happening, safety comes first. Keep a small amount of money and copies of key documents where only you can reach them, and talk to someone you trust, such as a women's group leader, a religious leader you trust, a lawyer, or a legal aid or women's support organisation in your state.
Next of kin, beneficiaries and wills

Every bank account, pension RSA and insurance policy lets you name a next of kin or beneficiary. Check these regularly, because an out-of-date name can delay money reaching your children. A **will** is a written document saying who should receive your property after death. Rules on wills and inheritance differ by state and can also be affected by customary and religious law, so it is wise to speak with a lawyer to make a valid will.
Protect your PIN and BVN

No bank, regulator or genuine agent will ask for your PIN, password or OTP. Do not let anyone, including family members, operate your accounts with your PIN. If you think someone knows it, change it in your bank app or at a branch immediately.
Start the conversation early
Talking about whose name is on property is easier when the relationship is calm. Frame it as protecting the children and the family's future, not as distrust.

Working with banks, cooperatives and advisers: ask, compare and complain
Ask the right questions before opening any financial product
Compare two savings offers by naira return and access

A good relationship with financial providers is a partnership: you bring your money and loyalty, and they should bring clear terms, safety and good service. Many people accept whatever the staff member says because they feel rushed or unsure. With a short set of questions, you can take control of every conversation, whether you are at a bank branch, talking to a fintech agent or joining a cooperative.
A woman using online banking on her phone
Whether in a branch or in an app, the same questions protect you.
Six questions before you sign
What is the total I will earn, or pay, in naira, and over what period?
What fees or charges apply, including account maintenance, transfer, card and early withdrawal charges?
How quickly can I get my money back, and is there a penalty for withdrawing early?
Who licenses or regulates this product, and can I see it on the regulator's website?
What happens if I miss a payment or the provider closes?
Can I have the terms in writing, or a link to them, before I agree?
If a staff member or agent cannot answer, or tells you not to worry about the details, take that as a reason to wait. A good product can be explained clearly.
Worked example: comparing two savings offers

For example, Grace has ₦300,000 she will not need for six months. Offer A is a bank fixed deposit at 12% a year for six months, with a penalty on early withdrawal. Offer B is a flexible savings wallet at 8% a year, withdraw any time. The rates are illustrative.
Offer A interest for six months: 300,000 × 0.12 × 6 ÷ 12 = ₦18,000.
Offer B interest for six months: 300,000 × 0.08 × 6 ÷ 12 = ₦12,000.
Difference: 18,000 minus 12,000 = ₦6,000 in favour of Offer A.
She asks both providers whether tax or charges are deducted from interest, and checks that the wallet's provider is licensed by the CBN.
She keeps one month of emergency money in Offer B and places the rest in Offer A.
Grace earns more on money she will not touch, while keeping emergency money flexible. She chose based on naira amounts and access, not on which advert looked better.
Checking a cooperative

Cooperatives can be excellent for savings and fair loans, and many WODDI members belong to one. A well-run cooperative is registered with the state's cooperative department, holds regular general meetings, keeps written records of every member's savings and loans, and has its accounts audited. Ask to see the registration certificate and the last annual report. Make sure every payment you make is recorded in your passbook or app the same day, and that money goes into an account in the cooperative's name, not a person's account.
Getting advice you can trust

Advice comes from many places: bank staff, agents, friends, social media influencers and group leaders. Before acting on it, ask two questions. First, **does this person earn money if I say yes?** A bank officer with a sales target or an agent paid per sign-up may be honest, but their advice is not neutral. Second, **can they show me the product's terms and licence?** Good advisers welcome questions and give you time to think. Be most careful with advice that arrives through WhatsApp or Telegram groups, comes with pressure to act today, or is backed only by screenshots of other people's profits.

Partnership also means checking your side. Read your account statement every month, even if only for five minutes. Look for charges you do not recognise, transfers you did not make and interest that was promised but not paid. Small errors found early are easy to fix, and your monthly check gives you the proof you need if you must complain.
When things go wrong: how to complain

Start with the provider. Put your complaint in writing, by email or through the official app, with your account name, dates, amounts and screenshots. Ask for a reference number. If the problem is not solved within the time the provider promises, or you get no answer, take it to the regulator for that type of product.

You now have the pieces: a balance sheet, a cash flow statement, five health numbers, a debt table, a protection pyramid and an asset register. A **Personal Financial Management Plan** puts them together in a few pages, so you can see the full picture and decide what comes next. It is also the capstone for this course.
A woman standing beside a board of personal goals
A written plan turns good intentions into dated actions.
What goes in the plan
**Page 1, where I stand**: your latest balance sheet and net worth, and your five health numbers.
**Page 2, how money moves**: a household budget built from at least one month of actual tracked income and spending, with planned and actual figures side by side.
**Page 3, my goal**: one savings goal with a target amount, a date and a record of progress.
**Page 4, protection**: your debt payoff order, your pyramid gaps and your register status.
**Page 5, my next 90 days**: three milestones with dates and the action for each.
The budget page: planned against actual

Your budget page is the working heart of the plan. It is built from your tracked month, not from guesses. Each line shows what you planned, what really happened and the difference. Below is a short illustrative extract.
Line
Planned
Actual
Difference
Food
₦7,000 over
Transport
₦1,500 under
Savings transfer
On plan
School fees share

You do not need every line to match. Look for the one or two lines with the biggest difference and ask why. Was food over because prices rose, because of visitors, or because shopping was not planned? The answer tells you whether to change the budget figure or change the habit. Next month's planned figures should reflect what you learned.
Writing a SMART goal

A **SMART** goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Save more money" is not SMART. "Save ₦150,000 for one month of essential costs by 31 August, by putting ₦25,000 into my separate savings account every month" is SMART. The amount comes from your health check, the date gives a deadline, and the monthly figure must fit inside your cash flow surplus.
Worked example: Funke's goal and 90-day plan

For example, Funke runs a small restaurant in Ibadan. Her health check showed emergency cover of two weeks and essential monthly costs of ₦180,000. Her cash flow surplus is about ₦40,000 a month. Amounts are illustrative.
Goal: one month of essential costs, ₦180,000. She already has ₦90,000 in easy-to-reach savings, so she needs 180,000 minus 90,000 = ₦90,000 more.
Time: at ₦30,000 a month, 90,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3 months. That leaves ₦10,000 of her ₦40,000 surplus as a margin for slow weeks.
Weekly amount: ₦30,000 × 12 months ÷ 52 weeks = about ₦6,923 a week, so she saves ₦7,000 every Monday.
Milestones: day 30, savings at ₦120,000; day 60, ₦150,000; day 90, ₦180,000.
Review: every Sunday evening she records the week's saving in her notebook and updates the total.
Funke's goal is specific, matches her real surplus and is broken into weekly actions. If she falls behind in one week, she can see it straight away and adjust the next week.
Your first 90 days
Day 1: plan written
Day 30: first milestone
Day 60: second milestone
Day 90: goal and review
Check progress at each milestone and adjust the next 30 days if needed.
Keeping the plan alive

Plans fail when they are written once and put away. Build three habits. **Weekly**, record income and spending and make your savings transfer on the same day. **Monthly**, compare planned and actual figures and note the biggest difference. **Quarterly**, update your balance sheet and five health numbers, and set the next 90-day goal. Each quarter's review is also the moment to move up the security pyramid: once your emergency cover goal is reached, the next goal might be clearing the most expensive debt or starting a Micro Pension contribution.

If a hard month comes, such as illness, a slow season or a family emergency, change the plan instead of abandoning it. Lower the monthly saving to a smaller amount you can keep, and write down the reason. A small saving you keep is worth more than a large one you abandon.
Share the plan with one accountability partner
Choose one trusted person, perhaps someone from your WODDI group, and agree to tell each other each month whether you reached your milestone. Share progress, not account details.
Keep your evidence
For the capstone you need your tracked month, your goal and progress record, and your 90-day plan. Photos of notebook pages or a simple spreadsheet are both fine.

Two women can each earn about 150,000 naira a month. One owns land and savings and owes nothing. The other owes a loan app and a cooperative. Same income, very different position.

Assets, liabilities, net worth
Anything you own with money value: cash, bank and wallet balances, cooperative savings, stock, land.
Any money you owe: a bank loan, a loan app balance, money from a relative, supplier credit, rent arrears.
Total assets minus total liabilities. It can be negative. It is a number to work on, not a judgement.

An asset is anything you own that has money value. Value it at what you could realistically sell it for this month, not what you paid. A freezer bought for 250,000 naira may only sell for about 120,000 today.
A liability is any money you owe, including money borrowed from family and stock taken on credit.
Net worth is what you own minus what you owe. A negative number is not a judgement. It is a clear number you can work on.

Your monthly cash flow statement
Moving money between your own accounts is not income or spending.
Collect a month's bank, wallet, cash records
Remove transfers between your own accounts
Group: money in, fixed, variable, occasional
Find your surplus or deficit
Calculate your savings rate
Step one. Open last month's statements in your bank and wallet apps, and add cash spending from your notebook.
Step two. Take out transfers between your own accounts, or you will count the same money twice.

Step three. Group everything. Occasional costs are the line people forget. School fees of about 180,000 naira a term are 540,000 a year, or 45,000 naira a month. Show that 45,000 every month and fees stop being a shock.
Step four. Money in minus all costs is your surplus or deficit. If there was a deficit, note how it was covered. A loan app is more urgent than a dip into savings.
Step five. Savings rate is money saved or used to reduce debt, divided by money in, times 100.
Aisha's February cash flow
For example, Aisha is a nurse in Kano who also sells perfume oils on WhatsApp.
Money in: salary and profit
Occasional costs, monthly share
Aisha builds her February statement from her bank app, her Moniepoint wallet and her notebook.
Her salary and perfume profit bring in 227,000 naira.
Fixed costs, including rent, data and a loan repayment, are 71,000 naira.
Variable costs like food and transport are 117,000 naira. Food is the biggest.
Her monthly share of school fees and gas is 24,000 naira.
That leaves a surplus of 15,000 naira. Adding the 25,000 she repaid on her loan, her savings rate is about 17.6%.
If your income changes a lot, plan fixed costs around your lowest month, not the average.
Health check
Five numbers, every quarter
Savings rate: is it positive?
Emergency cover: months of essential costs
Debt repayments as a share of income
Debt to assets: owe less than you own?
Net worth trend: is it rising?
Five numbers tell you what needs attention first. Is your savings rate positive?
Emergency cover is easy-to-reach savings divided by essential monthly costs. For example, Halima, a teacher in Abuja, had 45,000 naira against costs of 150,000. That is about nine days.
Debt repayment ratio shows how much income is already promised to lenders.
Debt to assets shows how much of what you own was paid for with borrowing.
And net worth trend shows whether your position is improving.
Take the first weak number as your only priority for three months. For Halima, that is emergency cover.
Keep your money safe
Protect your numbers
Do
Keep the notebook somewhere safe
Use a locked note on your phone
Download statements yourself
Never
Post balances in groups
Send statements to strangers
Share with loan 'helpers'
These numbers are private. Keep your sheet in a safe notebook or a locked note, and download statements yourself.
Bank statements show your account number and balances. Never send them to strangers, or to anyone who contacts you claiming to help with a loan.

Module 2 video
Interest, loans and protection: the tools of money
Interest, loans and protection: the tools of money.
This is the video for Module 2 of Financial Literacy and Personal Finance Management.
The arithmetic
Simple or compound interest?
Paid on the principal only
100,000 at 10% for 3 years
Ends at 130,000 naira
Interest earns interest too
Same 100,000 at 10% a year
Ends at 133,100 naira
Every loan and savings account runs on a few simple sums. Your phone calculator is enough.
Simple interest is paid only on the original amount, the principal. Save 100,000 naira at 10% a year for 3 years, and you earn 30,000. You end with 130,000 naira.
Compound interest is paid on the principal plus interest already earned. The same money grows to 110,000, then 121,000, then 133,100 naira.
Over 10 or 20 years the gap becomes very large. And compounding works against you in the same way when unpaid loan interest is added to what you owe.
Read the real cost
Small monthly rates, big yearly costs
2% a month: about 27% a year
4% a month: about 60% a year
10% a month: about 214% a year
Rule of 72: 72 / rate = years to double
Real return: growth after rising prices
Many loan apps quote a rate per month or per day. A small-looking number becomes very expensive over a year. 2% a month is about 27% a year with monthly compounding.
4% a month is about 60% a year.
And 10% a month is about 214% a year. Always ask: what is the total I will repay, in naira, and over how long?

To see how fast money doubles, divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 12%, about 6 years. If someone promises 30% a month, the money would double every few months. No legitimate business can do that. It is a classic sign of a Ponzi scheme.
Finally, check inflation. For example, Blessing earned 5% while prices rose 20%. Her balance grew by 10,000 naira, but she lost about 12.5% of her buying power.
Worked example
Two loan offers, both 5% a month
For example, Funmi needs 200,000 naira for stock and compares two 6-month offers.
Lender A, flat rate: total repaid
Lender B, reducing: total repaid
Illustrative offers. Ask every lender for the total.
With a flat rate, interest is charged on the full original amount for the whole loan. With a reducing balance, interest is charged only on what you still owe.
Lender A charges 5% a month flat. That is 60,000 naira in interest, so Funmi repays 260,000 naira.
Lender B charges 5% a month on a reducing balance. She repays about 236,421 naira.
Same quoted rate, but the flat-rate loan costs about 23,579 naira more. So compare loans by the total naira repaid, and ask for a repayment schedule before you sign.
Getting out of debt
Two ways to order your debts
List every debt with its balance, rate and minimum payment. Pay the minimum on all of them, then put extra money on one debt at a time.
Avalanche targets the highest rate first. A loan app at 8% a month costs 4,800 naira a month on 60,000, so it goes first.
Snowball clears the smallest balance first, for motivation. Either way, when one debt is cleared, add its payment to the next.
And your repayments are reported to credit bureaus licensed by the CBN, so paying on time builds your record.
Safety first
The FCCPC publishes approved digital lenders on its website. Check before you install any loan app.
Do not give a loan app access to your contacts or photos. Never pay an upfront fee to receive a loan.
Call your lender before a missed payment. Report harassment or threats to the FCCPC.
Before you borrow digitally, check that the lender is on the approved list published by the FCCPC.
Never give an app access to your contacts or photos, and never pay a fee to receive a loan.
If you will miss a payment, contact the lender before the due date and get any new arrangement in writing. Report harassment or threats to the FCCPC.
Protect what you build
Build your security from the bottom
Check the licence. Pay only into the company's registered account.
A hospital stay or a fire in a shop can take years of savings in a week. So build protection from the bottom. First, emergency savings.
Second, debt under control.
Third, insurance. Many people pay a small premium, and the pool pays the one who suffers a covered loss. NAICOM licenses insurers. Read what is excluded before you buy.
Fourth, a pension. If you are self-employed, PenCom's Micro Pension Plan lets you contribute amounts that suit you. For example, Comfort, a tailor, pays 5,000 naira a month.
Last, long-term investments such as government bonds or mutual funds, regulated by the SEC. Before you pay anyone, search the name on the matching regulator's website.
Key points
Remember
Turn monthly rates into yearly costs
Compare loans by total naira repaid
Pay all minimums, then target one debt
Check FCCPC, NAICOM, PenCom, SEC, CBN
Emergency savings first, investments last
To remember. Turn monthly rates into a yearly picture. Compare loans by total naira repaid. Pay all minimums, then target one debt.
Verify every provider with its regulator. And build from emergency savings upwards.

Your own money, smart questions and a 90-day plan
Your own money, smart questions, and a 90-day plan.
This is the video for Module 3 of Financial Literacy and Personal Finance Management.
Why this matters
Act, prove and protect your share
Many women build household money
Few have control or records of it
Independence is not secrecy
It means you can prove your share
Many women contribute to household money through salaries, trading, farming or unpaid work.
But when a marriage ends or a family dispute starts, a woman without her own account and records can lose what she helped build.
Financial independence does not mean keeping secrets from your partner.
It means you can act, prove and protect your share if you ever need to.
An account in my own name
My own phone for alerts
Tick each item. You need your NIN and BVN, an account in your own name with your own PIN, and alerts coming to your own phone.

Keep a register of every asset, whose name is on it and your share. For example, Amaka in Onitsha found she had contributed 800,000 naira of 2,000,000 for a plot, which is 40%. She photographed every receipt and kept copies safe.
And name a next of kin on every account, so money can reach your children without delay.
Safety first
Keep yourself and your money safe
No bank or genuine agent asks for your PIN, password or OTP. Do not let anyone use your accounts with it.
Taking all your earnings or forcing loans in your name is financial abuse. Safety comes first.
People pose as bank staff online and charge to fix complaints. Use only official contacts.
No bank, regulator or genuine agent will ask for your PIN or OTP. If you think someone knows it, change it immediately in your app or at a branch.

If a partner takes all your earnings, refuses you any money or forces loans in your name, that is financial abuse, not a normal disagreement. Keep some money and copies of documents where only you can reach them, and talk to someone you trust.
And beware people who pose as bank staff on social media. Use only contact details from the official website or app.
Before you sign
Six questions for any provider
If they cannot explain it clearly, wait.
Total earned or paid, in naira?
What fees and charges apply?
How fast can I get my money back?
Who regulates this product?
What if I miss a payment?
Can I have the terms in writing?
At a bank, a fintech or a cooperative, these six questions put you in control. First, what is the total I will earn or pay, in naira?
What fees apply, including maintenance, transfer and early withdrawal charges?
How quickly can I get my money back, and is there a penalty?
Who regulates it, and can I see it on the regulator's website?
What happens if I miss a payment? And can I have the terms in writing? If an agent tells you not to worry about the details, take that as a reason to wait.
Worked example
Grace compares two savings offers
Offer A: fixed
12% a year, 6 months
Penalty to withdraw early
Earns 18,000 naira
Offer B: flexible
8% a year
Withdraw any time
Earns 12,000 naira
For example, Grace has 300,000 naira she will not need for six months. A fixed deposit at 12% a year earns 18,000 naira in six months, but has a penalty for early withdrawal.

A flexible wallet at 8% earns 12,000 naira, and she can withdraw any time. She checks the wallet is licensed by the CBN, keeps one month of emergency money in it, and puts the rest in the fixed deposit. She chose by naira and access, not by the advert.
When things go wrong
Complain in writing, then escalate
First: the provider, in writing, get a reference
Banks and wallets: the CBN
Digital lenders: the FCCPC
Insurers: NAICOM
Pension administrators: PenCom
Investment firms: the SEC

Read your statement every month for charges or transfers you do not recognise. If something is wrong, complain to the provider in writing with dates, amounts and screenshots, and ask for a reference number.
If it is not solved, escalate to the right regulator. The CBN for banks and wallets, the FCCPC for digital lenders, NAICOM for insurers, PenCom for pensions and the SEC for investment firms.
Your plan
Funke's SMART goal
For example, Funke runs a small restaurant in Ibadan. Her essential costs are 180,000 naira a month.
Goal: one month of essential costs
Already in easy-to-reach savings
Still needed
Saved each month, for 3 months
Amounts are illustrative.

Your capstone is a Personal Financial Management Plan, and its heart is one SMART goal: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Funke's health check showed only two weeks of emergency cover.
She wants one month of essential costs, 180,000 naira. She already has 90,000.
So she needs 90,000 naira more.
Her surplus is about 40,000 naira a month, so she saves 30,000 and keeps 10,000 as a margin for slow weeks. That is about 7,000 naira every Monday.
Her milestones: 120,000 by day 30, 150,000 by day 60, and 180,000 by day 90. If a hard month comes, she lowers the amount instead of abandoning the plan.
Key points
Remember
An account and records in your own name
Never share your PIN, password or OTP
Ask six questions; get terms in writing
Complain in writing, then to the regulator
SMART goal, weekly action, 30-day milestones
To remember. Keep an account and records in your own name. Never share your PIN. Ask the six questions. Complain in writing first.
And turn your goal into weekly actions, then review weekly, monthly and quarterly.
